snapshot.content: Analysis · Key Differences and Use Cases

content.text: For immediate freshness, 'Versioned URLs', 'Purge by URL', and 'Surrogate-key purge' are most effective, but each has specific operational costs or limitations. 'TTL expiry' offers simplicity but sacrifices immediate freshness, while 'Stale-while-revalidate' prioritizes availability over strict freshness, with readers potentially seeing outdated content.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Comparing the techniques § text#1

content.text: Invalidation at the edge involves a set of trade-offs, not a single solution.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Conclusion § text#0

content.text: A reliable setup combines expiry times, explicit purges, deliberate stale serving, and versioned file names. Each component addresses the shortcomings of the others.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Conclusion § text#1

content.text: Short TTLs act as a safety net. Purges handle urgent corrections. Stale serving maintains site speed when the origin is under strain. Versioned names eliminate static assets from the invalidation problem.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Conclusion § text#2

content.text: Regardless of the chosen mix, be aware that purges reach different edge locations at varying times. Plan for a window of several seconds during which some users may still see the old version.

content.text: The fictional news site, Larkspur Media, serves as the ongoing example for this discussion.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge § text#4

content.text: This section introduces the critical problem of invalidating cached content at the edge for content-heavy sites. It highlights that while edge caching speeds up delivery, managing outdated content is complex and requires a layered approach of multiple techniques. The fictional site Larkspur Media is used as a practical example.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge § text#5

content.text: Every cached object has a Time To Live (TTL). Once the TTL expires, the edge either discards the copy or rechecks it with the origin.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Letting copies expire § text#0

reasons: the card cites no passage of the source

content.text: The origin sets the TTL using the
Cache-Control
header, e.g.,
Cache-Control: max-age=300
for a 300-second cache duration.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Letting copies expire § text#1

reasons: the card cites no passage of the source

content.text: TTL expiry requires no coordination between the origin and the edge, making it the default for CDNs.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Letting copies expire § text#2

reasons: the card cites no passage of the source

content.text: Upon TTL expiry, if the origin provided an
ETag
, the edge can revalidate the copy. If unchanged, the origin sends a
304 Not Modified
response, avoiding a full download.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Letting copies expire § text#3

reasons: the card cites no passage of the source

content.text: The main drawback of TTL is that it's a pre-determined guess. Changes at the origin before TTL expiry won't be reflected at the edge immediately.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Letting copies expire § text#4

reasons: the card cites no passage of the source

content.text: Shortening the TTL reduces the window for stale content but significantly increases traffic to the origin. For example, reducing an article's TTL from 300 to 30 seconds increased origin traffic by approximately eightfold.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Letting copies expire § text#5

reasons: the card cites no passage of the source

content.text: TTL-based caching is simple but can lead to stale content.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Letting copies expire § text#6

content.text: When content needs immediate change, the origin can ask the CDN to purge a specific URL. Larkspur's publishing system sends a purge for an article URL whenever an editor saves a correction.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#0

hints: source says "when content must change now"; the card says "whenever"
the card says "whenever"; the source doesn't

content.text: The purge removes the cached copy of the URL. The next request for that URL will then fetch fresh content from the origin.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#1

content.text: The origin calls the purge API with the URL. The API responds within about 150 milliseconds, but this only signifies that the request has been queued.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#2

content.text: The CDN's control plane distributes the purge request to all 90 edge locations.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#3

content.text: Each edge location marks its cached copy of the URL as invalid. Consequently, the next request to that location will result in a cache miss and will be directed to the origin.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#4

content.text: A purge request is accepted quickly, but it is not applied everywhere at the same moment. The CDN must deliver the purge to every edge location, and each location removes its copy on its own schedule. This means for a short period, some locations will serve the new version while others still serve the old one. Purging is eventually consistent, not instant.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#5

content.text: In Larkspur's measurements, half of the locations had applied a purge within 2 seconds, and the slowest location took 20 seconds. Until the last location has applied the purge, a reader routed to that location still gets the old copy.
From the source:
half

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#6

content.text: Purging by URL only removes the exact URL specified. For example, a corrected headline on an article page will not update on the home page, section page, or RSS feed unless those pages are also purged separately or their caches expire. Query strings further complicate this, as
/story/417?ref=social
is a distinct cache entry from
/story/417
and is not removed by purging the latter. Additionally, purge APIs are rate-limited; Larkspur's plan allows 1,000 purge calls per minute, which can be exhausted by bulk corrections.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#7

hints: source says "A corrected headline also appears on the home page, the section page and the RSS feed, and each of those cached pages keeps the old headline until it is purged separately or expires."; the card negates it
source says "Query strings make this worse, because `/story/417?ref=social` is a different cache entry from `/story/417` and is not removed by purging it."; the card drops the negation

content.text: The purging process is initiated by the origin, queued by the API, fanned out to CDN edge locations, and eventually invalidates cached content. The goal is to ensure users receive the most up-to-date content.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#8

content.text: The process is eventually consistent, not instant. There's a delay between the purge request and its application across all CDN edge locations, leading to a temporary state where different users might see different versions of content. Latency can be up to 20 seconds for the slowest locations.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by URL § text#9

content.text: The process doesn't explicitly branch or fail in the described flow, but its effectiveness is limited by its URL-specific nature and API rate limits. Content on related pages or with different query strings will not be purged automatically, requiring additional purge requests. Exceeding the rate limit (1,000 calls/minute for Larkspur) can prevent purges from being processed.

content.text: Surrogate keys allow the origin to label each response with tags, resolving the listing problem.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#0

content.text: The origin sends a
Surrogate-Key
header (e.g.,
Surrogate-Key: story-417 section-politics
), and the CDN records which cached objects are associated with these keys.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#1

hints: the card names "e.g"; the source doesn't

content.text: A single purge of a key (e.g.,
story-417
) removes all cached pages containing that story, including the article, home page, section page, and feed.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#2

hints: the card names "e.g"; the source doesn't

content.text: Keys can be granular, but each key adds to the header length. Larkspur limits responses to under 50 keys per response.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#3

hints: the card drops the caveat "but every key a page carries makes the header longer, and Larkspur keeps it under 50 keys per respo…"

content.text: The origin is responsible for tagging. A missing tag will result in a stale page without any error indication.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#4

content.text: Similar to URL purging, tag purges are delivered to each edge location independently, leading to a brief period where some locations serve updated pages while others serve old ones.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#5

hints: source says "a few seconds some locations serve the updated"

content.text: Tag purges can be extensive; for example, purging
section-politics
at Larkspur removes approximately 12,000 cached objects, causing a burst of cache misses at the origin.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#6

content.text: Surrogate keys enable efficient content purging by allowing the origin to tag cached objects. This shifts the responsibility of cache invalidation to the origin, but introduces challenges like potential stale content due to missing tags and temporary inconsistencies across edge locations during purge propagation. Large purges can also lead to significant cache miss bursts at the origin.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Purging by tag with surrogate keys § text#7

content.text: The
stale-while-revalidate

directive allows an edge location to immediately return an expired copy of content while fetching a fresh one from the origin in the background. This turns expiry from a waiting period into a background task.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#0

content.text: With
Cache-Control: max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=60
, if a request arrives after 300 seconds, the expired copy is returned immediately, and a fresh copy is fetched from the origin in the background.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#1

content.text: This approach provides a fast response to the current reader, and the subsequent reader receives the refreshed copy.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#2

content.text: Larkspur uses
stale-while-revalidate
on article pages where a minute of staleness is acceptable, but not for live election results.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#3

content.text: An expired copy is served for a maximum of 60 seconds past its Time-To-Live (TTL). After this period, the edge waits for the origin as it would for a regular cache miss.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#4

content.text: The
stale-if-error=86400
directive allows the edge to continue serving an expired copy for up to 86,400 seconds (one day) if the origin is returning errors.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#5

content.text: Serving stale content is a choice about tolerance for older data, not a method to make content fresher. It can hide a slow origin from readers.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#6

content.text: While it hides slow origins, serving stale content means some readers may see a copy older than what the TTL alone would suggest.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Serving stale on purpose § text#7

content.text: The most effective way to invalidate static assets is by assigning them a new name.

ai.stableNodeKey: Invalidating cached content at the edge › Versioned asset URLs § text#0

content.text: The build process incorporates a hash of each file's content into its name (e.g.,
app.3f9c2e.js
). This ensures that any change to a file results in a new URL, preventing requests for old cached versions.
